verses.note: Cain's question denies responsibility for his brother. Scripture's answer runs from the law's command to love the neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) to John's teaching that anyone who hates his brother is a murderer, while love lays down its life for the brothers (1 John 3:15-16).

When Peter asks how often to forgive, Jesus answers with seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22), the number of Lamech's vengeance in the Greek of Genesis. Many readers see a deliberate reversal: limitless forgiveness in place of limitless revenge.

The Bible's first use of the word love describes a father's love for his only son, and it appears in the command to give that son up. The New Testament echoes the pairing when it speaks of the Father's love for the Son and of God giving his only Son (John 3:16, 3:35).

The servant asks the family to imitate God: to show the chesed and emet that God has shown Abraham. In Scripture human loyalty is meant to mirror divine loyalty, as Micah 6:8 later puts it in asking Israel to love kindness.

The Bible's first statement that a husband loved his wife sits at the close of a story governed by God's providence. The love is personal and specific, and it follows a covenant commitment rather than preceding it.

The verse shows love willingly bearing cost. Jacob's service is not a burden resented but a price gladly paid, a human picture of the self-giving love Scripture describes as strong as death (Song of Solomon 8:6-7).

Jacob recognizes God's face in his brother's forgiveness. Scripture repeatedly ties the love of God to the love of the brother one can see (1 John 4:20), and this verse is one of its earliest pictures of that tie.

Joseph's compassion for Benjamin answers Jacob's prayer in verse 14 that God would grant mercy, rachamim, before the man. The prayer did not change a ruler's policy; it was answered in a brother's heart.
Judah argues from his father's love, not from Benjamin's innocence. He has come to see the father's bond with Rachel's son not as an injury to himself but as something worth guarding at his own cost.
Judah cannot bear to see his father's misery. Love for a father he once deceived now outweighs his own freedom.

Joseph's first act is to protect his brothers from public shame. He sends the Egyptians out before the old crime is named, so that the truth is spoken in private, among the family, where it can be forgiven.

Joseph's forgiveness is not only a refusal to punish but a positive commitment to his brothers' good and their children's. Forgiveness in Scripture moves beyond cancelling a debt to seeking the welfare of those forgiven (compare Luke 6:27-28).

Reuel's first question is where the stranger is and why he was left without a meal. The Old Testament treats hospitality to the stranger as a duty of righteousness (Genesis 18:2-5; Job 31:32), and here a fugitive with nothing receives it.
Love for God is commanded, which shows it is first a matter of loyalty and will, not of feelings that come and go. The threefold ‘all’ leaves no part of a person, including possessions, outside it.
Each example turns an imposition into an occasion of freely given service. The disciple is not defined by what others take but by what he chooses to give.
Love for enemies is not a strategy but a family likeness. Jesus prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34) and Stephen for those who stoned him (Acts 7:60).
Jesus does not forbid correcting a brother; he commands it to be done from humility. Galatians 6:1 applies the same pattern: restore the one caught in sin, watching yourself.
Paul says the same when he writes that love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:8-10). The rule makes love active and specific.
Jesus could have healed with a word, as he does elsewhere. He chooses to touch a man who may not have been touched in years, which makes the healing an act of restoration and not only of power.
God notices the smallest kindness done to Christ's people for Christ's sake. The verse gives weight to acts too small to be counted by anyone else.

Love for God is commanded, which shows that biblical love is more than feeling: it is the devotion of heart, life, mind, and strength, directed to God as the first act of obedience from which all others follow.

Love for neighbor is placed second, not optional. It flows from love for God and tests it (1 John 4:20). Luke follows the saying with the parable of the Good Samaritan, which removes any limit on who the neighbor is (Luke 10:29-37).

Love here is defined by action toward those who do not deserve it: doing good, blessing, praying. Jesus prays for his executioners (23:34) and Stephen for his (Acts 7:60), so the command is fulfilled first by its teacher.
Love of enemies is grounded in God's own character, not in its effectiveness. Children resemble their Father, and the Father is kind to those who are ungrateful to him.

The parable makes love the response to a debt cancelled, not the payment for it. Both debtors are equally unable to pay and equally forgiven; what differs is the size of the debt they know was released, and so the measure of their gratitude.

Jesus reads the woman's actions as love directed to him personally, and he measures Simon's coolness by the same standard. The scene quietly assumes that the right response to God's forgiveness is love for Jesus, a claim that places him where the parable placed the forgiving lender.

The last clause does not say that Simon needs little forgiveness. It says that one who thinks himself forgiven little will love little. The measure of love is a person's grasp of their own debt, which is why the parable is aimed at the host.

Jesus meets hostility with a rebuke to his own followers and a quiet change of route. Luke's Gospel then gives the Samaritans a place of honor: the Samaritan who shows mercy (10:33) and the Samaritan leper who returns to give thanks (17:16). John, who wanted fire for a Samaritan village, later prays for Samaritans to receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14-17).

Jesus speaks of wanting to gather Jerusalem ‘how often’, as if his longing reached back through the whole history of the prophets, and he uses a picture Scripture applies to God's own care (Deuteronomy 32:11, Psalm 91:4). The judgment that follows is announced by someone who grieves it.

The father's compassion moves before the confession. Love in this story is not a reward for repentance but the thing the returning son runs into, which is how the New Testament speaks of God's love coming first (Romans 5:8, 1 John 4:10).

The father's love for the older son is as patient as his love for the younger; he gives him the same assurance of belonging and the same invitation. The parable ends with an invitation left open, not a verdict.

The verse defines God's love by what it gave, and it names the object as the world, which in John is humanity turned away from God (1:10, 7:7). God's love does not wait for the world to become lovable.

The Father's love for the Son is the ground of the Son's work, not a reward for it. The relation between Father and Son is presented first as love, then as shared action, which is why John can later say that the love with which the Father loved the Son will be in believers (17:26).
Love for the Son is the sign of belonging to the Father. John makes the same argument in 1 John 5:1: everyone who loves the Father loves the one born of him.

The Gospel's second half begins with love, not power or glory, and names the recipients: his own who were in the world, the disciples who will betray, deny, and desert him. The love is complete (eis telos) before any of their failures are recorded.

The Gospel's chief witness is identified not by office or achievement but by being loved by Jesus. Whoever he was, the title presents discipleship as first of all receiving Christ's love, which every reader is invited to share.

Jesus' love is both the standard and the source of his disciples' love. The command asks them to love as those who have first been loved, which is why it comes after the foot washing and before the cross.

Love for Jesus is not measured by feeling alone but by keeping his word. The verse and its echoes in 14:21-24 make love and obedience inseparable without making either the price of the other, a theme 1 John 5:3 states plainly.

The love of the Father and the Son is not earned by obedience, since the Father loved the world before it loved him (3:16). But the verse speaks of a love that is known and enjoyed within a relationship of trust and obedience, and of a self-disclosure given to those who love him.

The love between the Father and the Son is the source of the disciples' love, and Jesus' own obedience is the pattern of theirs. Obedience does not earn the love; it is the way of remaining in a love already given, as a child remains in a father's love by living as his child.

The command to love one another is measured by the cross. The love Jesus asks for is not a feeling of affection but a readiness to give one's life for another, which 1 John 3:16 applies to the ordinary sharing of goods with a brother in need.

The Father loves the disciples himself. The verse removes any picture of a loving Son standing between his people and a distant Father: the love that sent the Son (3:16) is the love that receives those who come in his name.

The world is meant to see that the Father loves believers as he loves his Son. The love that has no measure (3:35) is the love with which the Father regards those who are in Christ, a claim that grounds the believer's assurance not in the believer's love but in God's.

The goal of all Jesus' revealing is that the Father's love for the Son be in believers. Knowledge of God's name is not an end in itself but the way that love is received, and the last words of the prayer are a promise of indwelling: and I in them.

The disciple who knows himself loved is the first to recognize the Lord. The Gospel does not set this against Peter's eager love, which throws him into the sea; it shows two kinds of devotion, one that perceives and one that runs, both drawn to the same person.

Jesus asks Peter about love, not courage or competence. The one who had boasted of greater loyalty than the others (Mark 14:29) now claims only what Jesus himself knows. Love for Christ is the root of the commission, and it is shown in feeding those who belong to him.
Hope rests on love. The believer's confidence that hope will not disappoint is grounded not in the strength of the hope but in the love of God, already given and experienced.
God's love precedes any change in the ones loved. It is not a response to human goodness but the cause of human reconciliation, as 1 John 4:10 says in similar terms.
‘Those who love God’ is rare in Paul as a description of believers (1 Corinthians 2:9, 8:3). Placed beside ‘called according to his purpose’, it shows that their love for God answers his prior call.
The cross is the proof that God is for his people. The argument from greater to lesser grounds confidence in all God's future gifts on the gift already given.
The victory belongs to Christ's love, not to the believer's strength. The past tense (‘who loved us’) anchors present confidence in what Christ has already done on the cross.
The love of God is ‘in Christ Jesus our Lord’. God's love is not a general benevolence but his love given and secured in his Son, which is why it cannot be lost.

Paul's wish reflects the love of Christ, who did become a curse for others (Galatians 3:13). Paul cannot take that place, but his willingness shows what Christlike love for the unbelieving looks like.

The cause of salvation is placed entirely in God's character: rich mercy and great love. The love is aimed at people just described as dead and under wrath, which is why Paul elsewhere says God showed his love while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8).

Love for God takes the concrete form of serving his people. The verse counts care for the saints as love shown ‘to his name’, the same logic as Jesus' words that what is done for the least of his brothers is done for him.
Love is something believers can provoke in one another. The verse gives the church a duty of mutual attention: to think about how to move one another toward love and good works.
